Basketball Data Science (Zuccolotto & Manisera, CRC 2020): a close reading

Source: BOOK_REVIEW.md

ggbasket started as a redesign of this book’s analyses; this note records that starting point. Covers what each chapter does, what holds up, and what to change. Page numbers are the book’s printed pages.

1. What the book is

The book is a statistics course built around one season (NBA 2017/18) and mostly one team (Golden State). Every analysis runs through the authors’ package BasketballAnalyzeR (Sandri). It has three levels:

Part Content Level
I. Ch. 1–2 Why data science in basketball; data types; possessions, pace, ratings, four factors; bar-line, radial, scatter and bubble plots; variability; Lorenz/Gini; shot charts introductory
II. Ch. 3 Association (χ², Cramér’s V, η², Pearson/Spearman); correlation matrix and network; MDS maps; assist networks; kernel densities of shots in time and space. FOCUS: CART on “high-pressure” shots (Serie A2 2015/16, Rio 2016) and a shot-making measure intermediate
II. Ch. 4 k-means (teams, GSW shots), Ward hierarchical clustering (players), BD/TD “explained variance”, CHI heterogeneity index. FOCUS: new player roles (TDA, SOM + fuzzy clustering) intermediate
II. Ch. 5 Simple linear regression, LOESS, Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoothing; scoring probability and expected points as functions of distance, shot clock and game time. FOCUS: GPS convex-hull “surface area” with Markov-switching and VAR models intermediate / expert
III. Ch. 6 The R package: data preparation (Kaggle box scores → Tbox/Obox/Pbox), customising ggplot objects, plotly technical

Datasets: Tbox, Obox (team and opponent totals), Pbox (players), Tadd (conference, playoffs) and PbP.BDB (BigDataBall play-by-play of the 82 GSW games, with shot coordinates, play length and lineups).

Philosophy. The opening “Marc Gasol is right” (p. 3) and Messina’s foreword set the tone: analytics supports a coach’s decisions and does not replace them. Three of Messina’s remarks become analyses in the book: - points against good vs bad teams → expected points by opponent tier, Fig. 5.8; - points early vs late → densities and scoring probability by game time, §3.5.1, §5.2.2; - who can hit the mid-range shot when the defence takes away the rim and the 3 → Fig. 5.6.

This “question first” framing is the book’s best feature, and ggbasket keeps it.

2. Chapter by chapter: what works and what doesn’t

Ch. 2: Basic statistics

Topic (book function) What it does Problems ggbasket fix
Possessions, pace, ORtg/DRtg, four factors (fourfactors) Kubatko et al. formulas: POSS = FGA + 0.44·FTA − ORB + TOV 0.44 is fitted to the NBA, not FIBA. Pace is “per minute”, so the axis reads 10.2–10.7. The four-factor bars are differences from the mean of the selected teams only (p. 25), so with 4 teams you learn nothing about the league four_factors(ft_coef=) gives pace per 48/40 by league; plot_four_factors() puts the selected teams in the whole-league distribution, right = better, with Oliver’s weights in the strip titles
ORtg and DRtg as two bar charts (Fig. 2.2) Two panels, each sorted alphabetically The trade-off between the two ratings can’t be seen plot_ratings(): ORtg × DRtg map, net-rating diagonals, quadrants
Bar-line plot (barline) Stacked bars + a line on a secondary y-axis Dual axes invite false comparisons (bar height vs line height). The bars ordered by plus-minus are shooting percentages, which don’t stack meaningfully plot_ranked(): stacked counts + an aligned dot column with its own axis
Radial plots (radialprofile) One common min–max axis for all variables; optional standardisation over the selected 9 players The authors flag the problems themselves (p. 30–33): area and variable order mislead, and the common scale flattens small-range stats (steals 0.029–0.052 on a 0.005–0.313 axis). Standardising over 9 hand-picked players makes “average” meaningless plot_profile(): percentiles within a reference group (league, position), so every axis is 0–100 and comparable. Bars by default, radar optional
Scatter / bubble (scatterplot, bubbleplot) Points labelled by case number, rainbow / blue–yellow–red palettes; bubble size rescaled 0–100 Case numbers make the reader cross-reference a table. Rescaled sizes hide units. Red–green palettes (Fig. 5.6) fail for colour-blind readers plot_quadrant(): mean cross, corner captions, repelled labels on highlights and extremes, size = area in real units, ColorBrewer RdBu / Okabe–Ito
Variability (variability) Range, CV, weighted CV; bubble diagram The 3P% example’s range (40 pts) is driven by Steven Adams 0/2 (p. 44). The book notes this but doesn’t fix it; raw small-sample percentages are the issue plot_spread() with shrink_rate(): empirical-Bayes beta-binomial shrinkage, weighted CV in the axis label
Inequality (inequality) Lorenz curve + Gini for top-n players One panel per team. The Gini depends on n (the book says to keep n fixed, p. 46) and on traded players plot_lorenz(): all teams on one panel (grey), extremes highlighted, Gini written on the plot. gini() reproduces the book’s 38.12%
Shot charts (shotchart) NBA court in feet; “sectors” are pie slices × distance rings, rainbow colour on e.g. play length; density polygons/raster/hexbin Sectors don’t follow court lines (the 3-point line cuts through them). There is no league baseline, so “50% here” has no reference. NBA only. Coordinates need manual rescaling plot_shot_zones(): real zones (rim, paint, mid L/C/R, corner 3s, above-break 3s) for NBA and FIBA geometry, coloured by FG% vs league (shrunk). plot_shot_hex(): size = frequency, colour = vs league from the same spot. plot_shot_density(compare=): density difference map

Ch. 3: Discovering patterns

  • Association measures (χ², Cramér’s V, η²). These are sound and well explained. But the GSW opponent × event-type table (Table 3.1) shows “significant but tiny” association (V = 0.06) and does not account for the unequal schedule (as the book admits). That is a lesson about effect size, and the book could say so more strongly.
  • η² of playoff qualification (Table 3.2). DRtg/ORtg explain about 40% and single box-score stats under 6%. This is a good point (“the game as a whole counts”). Net rating would explain far more and would close the argument.
  • Correlation matrix + network (corranalysis, Fig. 3.2). It uses ellipses, crosses for non-significant cells, no multiplicity correction, and a hard 0.5 threshold for the network. → plot_corr_matrix(): clustered order, Holm-adjusted significance shown by fading, coefficients printed.
  • Scatter-plot matrix by playoff group (Fig. 3.3). The claim that “players in better teams strengthen positive synergies” (p. 71) comes from eyeballing ~28 pairs of correlations with no uncertainty. With n ≈ 180 per group, the differences are within noise. Treat it as a hypothesis.
  • MDS (MDSmap). A Kruskal map plus four separate LOESS level plots to interpret it (Fig. 3.5). → plot_similarity_map(): one map with variable arrows (a biplot), PCA by default (more stable, reproducible) or MDS with stress reported.
  • Assist network (assistnet, Fig. 3.6–3.8). Kamada–Kawai layout changes with the seed, edge colour uses a white-blue-red scale, and node size and colour carry two more statistics. The “without Draymond Green” comparison (1.16 vs 1.11 points per shot, 10.8 vs 11.2 s) is on/off data confounded by lineups, opponents and garbage time, and has no uncertainty. → plot_assist_network() (fixed circular order by assists, width = count, colour = share of own baskets assisted) and plot_assist_matrix(), which is often clearer than any network.
  • Kernel densities in time (densityplot). Frequencies in three hand-set windows with “best scorer” labels. The windows (e.g. 4 ft / 18 ft) are arbitrary, and the reported shares (52% vs 49%) are within sampling noise. The book says so (“rather weak evidence”), which is good, but nothing quantifies it.
  • FOCUS: high-pressure shooting (CART). Its idea of grading each shot as made − P(make | situation) (eq. 3.1) is the most valuable in the book; it is today’s “shot-making over expected”. The implementation has weaknesses:
    • continuous predictors are cut into categories and fed to a single pruned tree, which is unstable;
    • shot location is reduced to “type” (2P/3P/FT), and no shooter effect is included;
    • P_i is unshrunk, so a 15-attempt threshold still leaves noisy rankings. → expected_fg() (logistic GAM on distance × angle per league and shot value, plus optional extra smooths such as shot clock or score margin) and shot_making() (FG% over expected, shrunk, points added) with plot_shot_making().

Ch. 4: Finding groups

  • k-means of teams (kclustering). Variables are ratios such as F1.r = eFG_off/eFG_def. The number of clusters is chosen from the elbow of BD/TD increments, 10 random starts are used, and clusters are labelled by radial plots + CHI. With 30 teams and 7 variables, five clusters means ~6 teams each. Cluster membership is not checked for stability, and the order of clusters changes between runs (hence set.seed(29)). → cluster_quality() (25 starts, silhouette as a second criterion) and plot_cluster_profiles() (a heatmap of cluster means in SD with n, CHI and the most typical members named).
  • k-means of GSW shots (points, distance, quarter time, play length). Clustering on points scored makes made/missed the dominant split. The book notices that four of six clusters are all-made or all-missed (p. 128) but doesn’t draw the conclusion: the outcome shouldn’t be a clustering input if the goal is to describe shot types.
  • Ward clustering of players. Per-game totals over 1,500+ minutes make the groups reflect minutes and usage as much as style. Per-36 or per-100 rates, plus shot-diet shares, give style clusters. The gallery example (16b_cluster_profiles) does this.
  • FOCUS: new roles. A good summary of Alagappan (TDA) and Bianchi et al. (SOM + fuzzy clustering). A natural modern extension is model-based clustering (Gaussian mixtures with uncertainty of membership) or a hierarchical Bayesian mixture.

Ch. 5: Modelling relationships

  • Simple regression (simplereg). TOV ~ AST and P3M ~ REB. The book correctly notes the violated assumptions (counts, negative predictions) and moves to LOESS. The useful output is the residual: who turns it over less than their assist load predicts. plot_fit() makes this the point by colouring by residual and naming the extremes.
  • Scoring probability and expected points (scoringprob, expectedpts). Nadaraya–Watson Gaussian kernel smoothing over distance, play length, period time and total time. These are the book’s most basketball-relevant charts, but:
    1. There is no uncertainty. Curve wiggles (e.g. “Draymond better in the second half”, the overtime bump in Fig. 5.8) may be noise.
    2. The kernel smooths across the 3-point line. The jump in shot value becomes a fake ramp (Fig. 5.6 shows expected points rising smoothly from ~15 ft to a hump at ~28 ft).
    3. Bandwidths are chosen by eye (bw = 300, 1200, 1500).
    4. Curves are drawn where there are almost no shots. Fig. 5.6 runs to 80 ft and dives to zero past half court.
    → shot_curve() adds bootstrap bands, split_value = TRUE (2s and 3s smoothed separately, keeping the discontinuity), a default bandwidth, and attempt density. plot_shot_curve() maps density to line width, so thin line = few shots.
  • FOCUS: surface area dynamics (Metulini et al.). Convex hull of 5 players from 80 Hz GPS, a two-regime Markov-switching model and a VAR on points. This is interesting and needs tracking data the project doesn’t have. Kept as a pointer only.

Ch. 6: The package

Good intentions: it works with ggplot objects and documents the data contract. Problems in the code style that the book teaches: - attach()/detach() everywhere; - subset() with long chains of Player == "A" | Player == "B"; - magic numbers (original_y/10 - 41.75); - capitalised mixed-case column names (P2p is a percentage in some tables and a proportion in others).

ggbasket uses lower-case columns, an o_ prefix for opponents, metres from the hoop, and as_ggbasket_*() converters so every book example still runs.

3. Problems that run through the whole book

  1. Uncertainty is never shown. No interval or band appears on any percentage, Gini, cluster mean, kernel curve or correlation difference. The text often then says “rather weak evidence”. The fix is simple: bootstrap bands, beta-binomial intervals and, for this project, Bayesian posteriors.
  2. Small samples are taken at face value. Shrinkage (empirical Bayes or hierarchical) is the standard remedy and fits the project’s brms/Stan goal.
  3. Everything is relative to the analysed subset. Four-factor differences from 4 teams, radial plots standardised over 9 point guards, η² on 30 teams. Comparisons should be relative to the league (or position), with the subset highlighted inside it.
  4. Per-minute, not per-possession. Player rates are per minute, so pace differences leak in. That matters for NBA vs EuroLeague comparisons (40 vs 48 minutes, different pace).
  5. One team, one season, one league. The book raises “space generalizability” (NBA ≠ Europe, p. 6) but never tests it. The NBA vs EuroLeague project does exactly that.
  6. Graphics. Some figures here make one or more of these mistakes:
    • rainbow or red–green palettes;
    • dual axes;
    • legends where direct labels would work;
    • case numbers as labels;
    • 9-panel radial grids;
    • default ggplot grey;
    • court sectors that ignore court lines.
    ggbasket’s rules:
    • lead with the story (title as finding, subtitle as encoding);
    • put the subject in context (grey league, coloured subject);
    • label directly;
    • use one diverging scale where red = better than average;
    • encode volume in size or line width so the eye goes where the data is.
  7. Causal language from observational splits. On/off assist networks, top vs bottom opponents, playoff vs non-playoff correlations. These are fine as descriptions and should be framed as such (or adjusted for lineup and opponent with a model).

4. From BasketballAnalyzeR to ggbasket

BasketballAnalyzeR ggbasket Main change
fourfactors() + plot() four_factors(), plot_ratings(), plot_four_factors() league context, net-rating map, FIBA pace
barline() plot_ranked() no dual axis
radialprofile() plot_profile(style = "bars" / "radar") percentiles in a reference group
scatterplot(), bubbleplot() plot_quadrant(), plot_fit(), plot_corr_matrix() direct labels, residual story, Holm-adjusted significance
variability() plot_spread(), shrink_rate() shrinkage of small samples
inequality() lorenz(), gini(), plot_lorenz() all teams in one panel
shotchart() plot_shot_zones(), plot_shot_hex(), plot_shot_density(), geom_court(), shot_zone() real zones, NBA + FIBA, vs-league colour, metres
densityplot(), scoringprob(), expectedpts() shot_curve(), plot_shot_curve() bootstrap bands, split at the 3-point line, density as line width
CART shot-making (FOCUS 3.6) expected_fg(), shot_making(), plot_shot_making() GAM expected FG%, shrunk FG% over expected
corranalysis() plot_corr_matrix() clustered order, Holm
MDSmap() plot_similarity_map() biplot arrows instead of level plots
kclustering(), hclustering() cluster_quality(), plot_cluster_quality(), plot_cluster_profiles() silhouette, one heatmap with typical members
assistnet() assist_network(), plot_assist_network(), plot_assist_matrix() stable layout, matrix view
PbPmanipulation() + manual rescaling as_ggbasket_teams/players/shots() converters into one convention
Cramer’s V, eta-squared (Sec. 3.1, no BAR function) association(), plot_association() all three indices on one 0-1 heatmap, index named in each cell
Assist Gini per player (Sec. 3.4) assist_network() (ast_gini, recv_gini, partners), plot_assist_roles() hub vs two-man-game map
Joint density (Sec. 3.5.3, ggpairs) plot_joint() filled 2-D density + marginals + labelled players
High-pressure CART (Sec. 3.6) pressure_situations(), pressure_effects(), plot_pressure() logistic model with expected FG% offset, effects in percentage points with intervals; shot clock estimated from play-by-play
(not in the book) player_rates(), expected_wins(), plot_luck() TS%, usage, AST%, rebound/steal/block/turnover rates; Pythagorean wins and luck

Not covered: the GPS/convex-hull spacing analysis of Section 5.3 (needs player-tracking data) and the self-organising-map / topological roles mentioned in Chapter 4 (a mixture model, Section 5 below, is the better tool).

5. Where to take it next (Bayesian, to match the project’s learning goal)

  1. Hierarchical shooting. made ~ 1 + (1 | player) per zone with brms (beta-binomial or logit). This is the full-Bayes version of shrink_rate(). Posterior intervals then show on every percentage and zone chart.
  2. xFG with a shooter effect. made ~ s(dist, angle, by = league) + (1 | player) + (1 | defender_team). The player random effect is shot-making over expected, with honest uncertainty. It replaces the book’s CART + P_i.
  3. Shot surface per league. A 2-D Gaussian-process or t2() tensor smooth of FG% over the court, NBA vs EuroLeague. RQ1 already does a version.
  4. Uncertain clusters. A Gaussian mixture in brms/Stan (or mclust) gives each player a membership probability (“60% stretch big, 40% wing”), which is what the book’s FOCUS on new roles wants.
  5. Lead-lag style. Combine plot_profile() percentiles with the RQ4 “ahead of their time” smoothed path.
